relevance_reason: Reports two Japanese siblings with CAMRQ4 and compound heterozygous ATP8A2 variants, one of them novel.

findings.statement: Narishige et al. (2022) reported 2 Japanese siblings with CAMRQ4 who presented with athetotic movements at 1 and 2 months of age. They also had ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, feeding difficulty, hypotonia, and severely delayed development. One sib had retinal degeneration and optic atrophy. Flattening of auditory brainstem responses and areflexia developed later. At last follow-up, neither patient could sit or achieve head control, although some nonverbal communication was preserved.
quotes: Japanese siblings presented with athetotic movements at 1 and 2 months of age. They also had ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, feeding difficulty, hypotonia, and severely delayed development. One patient had retinal degeneration and optic atrophy.
Flattening of the auditory brainstem responses and areflexia developed. At the last follow-up, neither patient could sit or achieve head control, although some nonverbal communication was preserved.

phenotypes.text: inability to sit or achieve head control

findings.statement: In 2 Japanese sibs with CAMRQ4, Narishige et al. (2022) identified compound heterozygous nonsense variants in the ATP8A2 gene by whole-exome sequencing: c.1741C>T (p.Arg581Ter), which had been previously reported, and c.2158C>T (p.Arg720Ter), which was novel.
quotes: Whole exome sequencing revealed compound heterozygous variants of ATP8A2: NM_016529.6:c.[1741C>T];[2158C>T] p.[(Arg581*)];[(Arg720*)]. The p.(Arg581*) variant has been reported, while the variant p.(Arg720*) was novel.

findings.statement: Narishige et al. (2022) noted that symptoms did not progress in early development, making CAMRQ4 difficult to distinguish from dyskinetic cerebral palsy, particularly in solitary cases, but suggested that visual and hearing impairments associated with involuntary movements and severe developmental delay may be a clue to suspect CAMRQ4.
quotes: The symptoms did not progress in the early period of development, which makes it difficult to distinguish from dyskinetic cerebral palsy, particularly in solitary cases.
However, visual and hearing impairments associated with involuntary movements and severe developmental delay may be a clue to suspect CAMRQ4.

relevance_reason: Reports two siblings with congenital ataxia and a homozygous ATP8A2 splice variant with minigene functional evidence, which broadens the CAMRQ4 phenotype.

findings.statement: Damásio et al. (2021) described 2 sibs with congenital ataxia who learned to walk on their own by age 4 years. After 16 years of follow-up, they had near-normal cognition, cerebellar ataxia, mild pyramidal signs, and dystonia.
quotes: we describe two siblings with congenital ataxia, who acquired independent gait by age 4 years. After 16 years of follow-up they presented near normal cognition, cerebellar ataxia, mild pyramidal signs, and dystonia.

findings.statement: In 2 sibs with congenital ataxia, Damásio et al. (2021) used exome sequencing to identify a novel homozygous variant in intron 17 of the ATP8A2 gene (c.1580-18C-G). Bioinformatics tools predicted that it creates a new acceptor splice site. In a minigene assay in HEK293T cells, the variant construct produced an aberrant transcript that kept 17 bp of intron 17 because an alternative acceptor splice site was used. This inserted 4 amino acids and created a premature stop codon. The authors concluded that the variant was disease-causing.
quotes: On exome sequencing, a novel homozygous variant (c.1580-18C > G - intron 17) in ATP8A2 was identified. A new acceptor splice site was predicted by bioinformatics tools, and functionally characterized through a minigene assay.

The construct with the c.1580-18C > G homozygous variant produced an aberrant transcript, leading to retention of 17 bp of intron 17, by the use of an alternative acceptor splice site, resulting in a premature stop codon by insertion of four amino acids.

findings.statement: Damásio et al. (2021) concluded that their findings expand ATP8A2-related disorders to include less severe forms of congenital ataxia.
quotes: These results allowed us to establish this as a disease-causing variant and expand ATP8A2-related disorders to include less severe forms of congenital ataxia.

relevance_reason: Reports a consanguineous Iranian family with CAMRQ4 and a novel homozygous ATP8A2 missense variant segregating with disease.

findings.statement: Mohamadian et al. (2020) described 3 sibs (a 9-year-old girl proband, a 15-year-old sister, and a 17-year-old brother) from a consanguineous Iranian family of Arab descent born to healthy first-cousin parents, with non-progressive cerebellar ataxia, severe hypotonia, intellectual disability, dysarthria, and cerebellar atrophy. The proband had severe neonatal hypotonia, global psychomotor delay, feeding difficulties since infancy, and was wheelchair-bound, unable to walk, sit, or hold her head. All 3 patients had IQ of 20 to 40, delayed speech with dysarthria, absent deep tendon reflexes, and cerebellar atrophy on brain MRI; hearing was normal, there were no seizures or optic atrophy, and metabolic investigations were normal.
quotes: The proband (Ⅳ. 4) was a 9‐year‐old girl from healthy and first‐cousin parents with Arab descent (Figure 1A).

The first noticeable clinical sign was severe neonatal hypotonia. Afterward, she demonstrated a lag in all psychomotor and developmental milestones. In the aspect of motor performance assessment, she was wheelchair‐bound and could not walk, sit, or hold her head.

All 3 patients had limited intellectual functioning with IQ levels ranging from 20 to 40. Also, they had delayed speech and language as well as signs of dysarthria. Nevertheless, the hearing examination of patients was not shown any significant impairment. In these patients, deep tendon reflexes were absent.

findings.statement: In 3 affected sibs from a consanguineous Iranian family with CAMRQ4, Mohamadian et al. (2020) identified a homozygous c.1339G-A transition (NM_016529.6) in exon 14 of the ATP8A2 gene, resulting in a gly447-to-arg (G447R) substitution at an extremely conserved residue in the ATP-binding (N) domain. The variant, found by whole-exome sequencing after normal karyotype and chromosomal microarray, was confirmed by Sanger sequencing and segregated with disease: parents and 2 unaffected sibs were heterozygous and 1 unaffected sib was wildtype. It was absent from public databases and 100 ethnically matched controls. Structural modeling predicted reduced protein stability and an altered ligand-binding pocket.
quotes: only one homozygous missense variant “NM_016529.6:c.1339G > A, NP_057613.4:(p.Gly447Arg)” in exon 14 of the ATP8A2 gene on 13q12.1 was predicted as pathogenic

According to segregation analysis, the sequence variant was homozygous in the affected individuals (Ⅳ0.1, Ⅳ0.2, Ⅳ0.4) (Figure 1C) and heterozygous in the parents (Ⅲ. 1, Ⅲ. 2), one healthy brother (Ⅳ. 3), and one healthy sister (Ⅳ. 5) (Figure 1D).
The identified novel variant was not found in 100 healthy and ethnically matched controls.

findings.statement: Mohamadian et al. (2020) predicted by homology modeling that the G447R substitution in ATP8A2 severely reduces protein stability (FoldX ddG 7.94 kcal/mol) and alters the ligand-binding pocket adjacent to the active site, which may decrease ligand-binding affinity and catalytic activity; they suggested it could also disrupt folding and interaction with CDC50A (TMEM30A).
quotes: About the FoldX algorithm prediction, the substitution of Glycine to Arginine at position 447 results in a severely reduced protein stability with ddG of 7.94 kcal/mol.
According to 3DLigandSite output, the amino acid residue 447 is adjacent to the active site, and mutation p.G447R affected the ligand‐binding pocket.
It means that the substitution of p.G447R in ATP8A2 could make changes in folding, expression, and flippase activity of ATP8A2 by disrupting its interaction with CDC50A.

relevance_reason: The paper describes the first family with CAMRQ, the cerebellar ataxia/quadrupedal locomotion syndrome, caused by a homozygous ATP8A2 missense variant. This makes it the defining report for CAMRQ4.

findings.statement: Onat et al. (2013) studied a consanguineous Turkish family in which 4 members had cerebellar ataxia, mental retardation, and dysequilibrium syndrome with quadrupedal locomotion and cerebellar atrophy.
quotes: We investigated a consanguineous family from Turkey with four affected individuals exhibiting the condition.
Missense mutation in the ATPase, aminophospholipid transporter protein ATP8A2 is associated with cerebellar atrophy and quadrupedal locomotion.

phenotypes.hpo_label: Cerebellar ataxia associated with quadrupedal gait

findings.statement: Onat et al. (2013) used homozygosity mapping in the consanguineous Turkish family and found several homozygous regions shared by affected members, including one on chromosome 13q12.
quotes: Homozygosity mapping revealed that several shared homozygous regions, including chromosome 13q12.

findings.statement: In the affected members of a consanguineous Turkish family with CAMRQ, Onat et al. (2013) identified a novel missense variant in the ATP8A2 gene, p.I376M. They found it by targeted next-generation sequencing of one affected individual, followed by segregation analysis, population screening, and prediction approaches. The variant lies in a highly conserved C-terminal transmembrane region of the E1 E2 ATPase domain.
quotes: Targeted next-generation sequencing of an affected individual followed by segregation analysis, population screening and prediction approaches revealed a novel missense variant, p.I376M, in ATP8A2.
The mutation lies in a highly conserved C-terminal transmembrane region of E1 E2 ATPase domain.

findings.statement: Onat et al. (2013) noted a previously identified unrelated individual with mental retardation and severe hypotonia who carried a de novo balanced t(10;13) translocation that disrupted the ATP8A2 gene.
quotes: Interestingly, an unrelated individual has been identified, in whom mental retardation and severe hypotonia is associated with a de novo t(10;13) balanced translocation resulting with the disruption of ATP8A2.

findings.statement: Onat et al. (2013) noted that ATP8A2 is expressed mainly in the brain and during development, particularly in the cerebellum. They suggested that ATP8A2 is involved in the development of the cerebro-cerebellar structures that humans need for posture and gait.
quotes: The ATP8A2 gene is mainly expressed in brain and development, in particular cerebellum.
These findings suggest that ATP8A2 is involved in the development of the cerebro-cerebellar structures required for posture and gait in humans.

relevance_reason: Original report identifying a homozygous WDR81 missense mutation in a consanguineous Turkish family with cerebellar hypoplasia, intellectual disability and quadrupedal locomotion (CAMRQ4).

findings.statement: Gulsuner et al. (2011) studied a large consanguineous Turkish family with an extremely rare phenotype of quadrupedal locomotion, mental retardation, and cerebro-cerebellar hypoplasia. Diffusion-weighted imaging and fiber tractography showed morphologic abnormalities of the cerebellum and corpus callosum, particularly atrophy of the superior, middle, and inferior cerebellar peduncles; structural MRI showed additional morphometric abnormalities in cortical areas including the corpus callosum, precentral gyrus, and Brodmann areas BA6, BA44, and BA45.
quotes: We investigated a large consanguineous family from Turkey exhibiting an extremely rare phenotype associated with quadrupedal locomotion, mental retardation, and cerebro-cerebellar hypoplasia

Diffusion weighted imaging and fiber tractography of the patients' brains revealed morphological abnormalities in the cerebellum and corpus callosum, in particular atrophy of superior, middle, and inferior peduncles of the cerebellum.
Structural magnetic resonance imaging showed additional morphometric abnormalities in several cortical areas, including the corpus callosum, precentral gyrus, and Brodmann areas BA6, BA44, and BA45.

phenotypes.hpo_label: Cerebellar ataxia associated with quadrupedal gait

findings.statement: By homozygosity mapping in a large consanguineous Turkish family, Gulsuner et al. (2011) linked the disorder to a 7.1-Mb region of homozygosity on chromosome 17p13.1-p13.3.
quotes: linked to a 7.1-Mb region of homozygosity on chromosome 17p13.1-13.3

findings.statement: By targeted sequencing of the entire homozygous region in 3 affected individuals and 2 obligate carriers from a consanguineous Turkish family, Gulsuner et al. (2011) identified a private homozygous missense mutation in WDR81 (P856L) that cosegregated with the condition in the extended family. The mutation lies in a highly conserved region of WDR81, flanked by an N-terminal BEACH domain and C-terminal WD40 beta-propeller domains.
quotes: Targeted sequencing of the entire homozygous region in three affected individuals and two obligate carriers uncovered a private missense mutation, WDR81 p.P856L, which cosegregated with the condition in the extended family.
The mutation lies in a highly conserved region of WDR81, flanked by an N-terminal BEACH domain and C-terminal WD40 beta-propeller domains.

findings.statement: Gulsuner et al. (2011) reported that WDR81 is predicted to be a transmembrane protein and is highly expressed in the cerebellum and corpus callosum, particularly in the Purkinje cell layer of the cerebellum.
quotes: WDR81 is predicted to be a transmembrane protein. It is highly expressed in the cerebellum and corpus callosum, in particular in the Purkinje cell layer of the cerebellum.

findings.statement: Gulsuner et al. (2011) noted that WDR81 was the third gene, after VLDLR and CA8, implicated in quadrupedal locomotion in humans.
quotes: WDR81 represents the third gene, after VLDLR and CA8, implicated in quadrupedal locomotion in humans.

relevance_reason: Only the title is available. It is a reply letter about genetic heterogeneity of cerebellar hypoplasia with quadrupedal locomotion, which is the phenotype group that includes CAMRQ4. With no details, it supports only a heterogeneity note.

findings.statement: In a reply to Herz et al. and Humphrey et al., Ozcelik et al. (2008) discussed genetic heterogeneity of cerebellar hypoplasia with quadrupedal locomotion.
quotes: Genetic heterogeneity of cerebellar hypoplasia with quadrupedal locomotion

phenotypes.hpo_label: Cerebellar ataxia associated with quadrupedal gait

relevance_reason: Only the title ("Devolution" of bipedality) was available. It points to a commentary on quadrupedal locomotion, which is part of the CAMRQ phenotype, but the title alone has no patient, variant or mechanistic content that could back a finding.

Only the title is available. It shows the paper is about genes and quadrupedal locomotion in humans, which is the subject of the CAMRQ entries. It appears to be a PNAS letter. Without an abstract or full text, no specific patients, variants or conclusions can be pulled out and backed by quotes.

The abstract mainly reports VLDLR mutations (CAMRQ1) in two Turkish families. It is relevant to CAMRQ4 only because it reports two other consanguineous Turkish families (B and C) with quadrupedal gait whose phenotype was not linked to chromosome 9p, which shows genetic heterogeneity. The abstract does not identify a CAMRQ4 gene.

findings.statement: Ozcelik et al. (2008) studied 4 large consanguineous Turkish kindreds with quadrupedal gait (Unertan syndrome). In 2 families (B and C), the phenotype was not linked to chromosome 9p, where VLDLR mutations had been found in families A and D. The authors concluded that hereditary disorders with quadrupedal gait in humans are genetically heterogeneous.
quotes: In two other families (B and C), the phenotype is not linked to chromosome 9p.
hereditary disorders associated with quadrupedal gait in humans are genetically heterogeneous

phenotypes.hpo_label: Cerebellar ataxia associated with quadrupedal gait

findings.statement: Ozcelik et al. (2008) described 4 large consanguineous kindreds from Turkey with quadrupedal gait (Unertan syndrome), which they described as a rare phenotype associated with dysarthric speech, mental retardation, and varying degrees of cerebrocerebellar hypoplasia.
quotes: Quadrupedal gait in humans, also known as Unertan syndrome, is a rare phenotype associated with dysarthric speech, mental retardation, and varying degrees of cerebrocerebellar hypoplasia. Four large consanguineous kindreds from Turkey manifest this phenotype.

phenotypes.hpo_label: Cerebellar ataxia associated with quadrupedal gait
